title: Using Claude to Write an Open-Source Driver Draws a $25,000 Claim Threat from Synaptics

content_html:
A small personal hobby project has been backed into a corner by a legal letter from a chip giant. Synaptics recently sent a cease-and-desist letter to Lothian, an open-source enthusiast developing the "Vino" driver, demanding that he stop, take down, and destroy this Linux driver that provides open-source support for DisplayLink devices—and when he was writing the code, he even had Claude AI as a helper.

A Reverse-Engineered Open-Source Alternative—Who Did It Threaten?

DisplayLink technology uses USB to connect external monitors to computers. Although Synaptics offers Linux support, it requires bundling closed-source proprietary components. Lothian's Vino takes an independent reverse-engineering route, uses Claude to assist development, and got it working on a Dell D6000 docking station. He had hoped to get the work merged into the Linux kernel. This hit a nerve at Synaptics: Andrew Bateman, its head of legal, said bluntly that making the implementation public would help competitors understand its proprietary technology and weaken its advantage.

The Patent Hammer, Priced by the Week

Synaptics accuses Vino of infringing two UK patents (GB2484736 and GB2485613). It not only demands deletion of the code, documentation, and materials submitted to kernel maintainers, but also threatens that if he does not comply by the deadline, it will seek $25,000, and another $25,000 every seven days after that. Lothian counters that he is just an individual hobbyist, has not infringed, and questions the validity of both patents—some of the technology was already public before they were filed. The Vino repository has now been made private, and the related letters and replies have been sent to the Linux kernel mailing list, turning the matter into a public dispute for the open-source community to watch.
